snapshot.title: UPSC History: Non-Cooperation & Chauri Chaura
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1920: NCM starts. 1922: Chauri Chaura ends it. Nagpur session: INC shift. Khadi promoted. Foreign cloth burnt.

quick_notes.title: Launch of NCM (1920)
quick_notes.detail: Approved at Nagpur session (1920). Objectives : Self-government (Swaraj), redressal of Punjab wrongs, support to Khilafat.
quick_notes.explanation: The Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM) was a major nationwide protest against British rule in India, officially approved at the Indian National Congress session held in Nagpur in December 1920. Its main goals were three: first, to achieve Swaraj, which means self-rule or complete independence from Britain; second, to demand justice for the wrongs committed by the British in Punjab, specifically the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919; and third, to support the Khilafat movement, which was a campaign by Indian Muslims to protect the Ottoman Caliphate (the religious leader of Sunni Muslims) after World War One. To achieve these aims, the movement asked Indians to peacefully refuse to cooperate with the British government by boycotting British goods, courts, schools, and government jobs.

quick_notes.title: Program of Action
quick_notes.detail: Surrender of titles (Gandhi gave back Kaiser-i-Hind). Boycott of govt schools, courts, and foreign cloth. Promotion of Khadi and Charkha. National schools like Jamia Millia and Kashi Vidyapeeth founded.
quick_notes.explanation: The Program of Action was a set of activities planned during the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) led by Mahatma Gandhi. As part of this program, Indians were asked to surrender British titles of honour, such as the Kaiser-i-Hind (a medal and title given by the British for public service); Gandhi himself returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal. People were also asked to boycott (refuse to use or participate in) government-run schools, government courts, and foreign-made cloth. Instead, they were encouraged to promote Khadi (hand-spun, hand-woven cloth) and the Charkha (spinning wheel) to make their own cloth. New national schools, like Jamia Millia Islamia in Delhi and Kashi Vidyapeeth in Varanasi, were founded as Indian alternatives to British-run institutions.

quick_notes.title: Chauri Chaura (Feb 5, 1922)
quick_notes.detail: A violent clash in Gorakhpur district where a mob burnt a police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi, a staunch believer in non-violence, immediately suspended the movement.
quick_notes.explanation: Chauri Chaura was a violent incident that happened on February 5, 1922, in the Gorakhpur district of present-day Uttar Pradesh. In this clash, a mob of protesters burned down a police station and killed 22 policemen. Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of the Indian independence movement who strongly believed in non-violence as a principle, immediately called off the Non-Cooperation Movement after hearing about this event. Non-violence means refusing to use physical force to achieve political goals. The Non-Cooperation Movement was a campaign Gandhi had launched in 1920 to resist British rule through peaceful means like boycotting British goods and institutions. By suspending the movement, Gandhi showed that he would not tolerate any violence in the name of freedom.

quick_notes.title: Impact of Withdrawal
quick_notes.detail: Shocked many leaders like Nehru and Subhas Bose (who called it a "national calamity"). Led to a lull in the movement and the rise of internal divisions.
quick_notes.explanation: The withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922, which was a campaign where Indians refused to cooperate with British rule, shocked many leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose, with Bose calling it a "national calamity," meaning a great disaster for the country. This withdrawal happened because the movement was called off by Mahatma Gandhi after a violent incident in Chauri Chaura, where protesters killed police officers, and Gandhi felt the movement was not ready for non-violent discipline. As a result, the movement went into a lull, which is a quiet or inactive period, and this led to the rise of internal divisions, meaning disagreements and splits among Indian leaders about what strategy to use next for independence.

quick_notes.title: Economic Impact
quick_notes.detail: Import of foreign cloth fell by half. Indian textile mills and handlooms got a massive boost.
quick_notes.explanation: During the early 20th-century Swadeshi Movement (a campaign to boycott British goods and use only Indian-made products), the import of foreign cloth from Britain fell by half. This happened because Indians stopped buying British textiles and instead purchased cloth made in Indian textile mills (large factories that use machines) and handlooms (traditional looms operated by hand by weavers in villages). As a result, both the modern factory-based textile industry and the traditional handloom sector experienced a massive boost in demand and production. The term "foreign cloth" specifically means textiles manufactured outside India, mainly in Britain, which had dominated the Indian market before this movement.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'First Mass Strike'. The Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM) was Gandhi's first pan-India struggle, launched in 1920 to undo the 'Punjab Wrongs' and support the Khilafat cause. It saw the surrender of titles, boycott of schools, and the rise of the 'Charkha'. For UPSC, focus on the 'Program of NCM' and the controversial withdrawal after the 'Chauri Chaura' incident. This movement changed the nature of the Indian freedom struggle forever.
